### Observed differences

- **Resource allocation became more concentrated.** In the earlier window, assignments of A01, A03, A17 and A22 were spread thinly over many users: the pooled share of assignees outside the ten most frequent was about 47–55 in 100 assignments per activity, and no single user held more than about 9 in 100. In the later window, a small group took a larger share: User_3, previously outside the ten most frequent assignees, became the most frequent assignee for all four activities (about 11–13 in 100), User_39 and User_53 also gained (User_39 to about 7–9 in 100), and the pooled remainder fell by roughly 10–13 points to about 35–45 in 100. Each of the four allocation profiles differs more than in about 99.9% of random re-splits of the pooled data. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004]

- **Offer creation repeated less often.** A13 and A14 still appeared in every trace in both windows, but their mean occurrences per trace fell from about 1.48 to about 1.26 (roughly 15% fewer), and the share of traces in which they repeated fell from about 34 in 100 to about 20 in 100. The two items show identical values, so they most likely reflect one underlying behaviour rather than two independent changes. [OCC001, OCC002]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the possibility that the allocation of work across resources changed: in the later window, assignments of A01, A03, A17 and A22 shifted from a diffuse distribution over many occasional assignees to a more concentrated pattern in which a small group of users — including User_3, User_39 and User_53 — took over roughly the share previously held by the long tail, whose pooled share fell by about 10–13 assignments in 100 per activity. Supporting signs: all four activity-level allocation profiles moved in the same direction with the same users gaining; the resource family produced 4 qualifying items against about 0.006 expected without change, so chance alone cannot account for the family as a whole; and the activities remained in use at comparable levels in both windows (for example, A01 assignments in 200 of 200 traces before and after). Limitations: the resource codes are anonymous, so no roles, people or teams can be inferred, and the four items may describe one underlying reallocation rather than four independent changes. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004]

A competing explanation the evidence cannot rule out is a shift in the mix of cases — the reduced repetition of offer creation hints at some case-mix change — which could indirectly change which users handle the work rather than reflecting a direct change in assignment practice. [OCC001, OCC002]

Other differences: the decreased repetition of A13 and A14 (mean occurrences per trace about 1.48 → 1.26; traces with repetition about 34 → 20 in 100, while participation stayed at 100%). The control-flow family produced 2 items against about 0.21 expected without change, which is what an unchanged process typically produces, so this repetition decrease is not established as a change and may be sampling variation. [OCC001, OCC002]
